at-alcohol-01.question: In Austria, from which blood alcohol level does § 5(1) StVO deem a driver's condition 'in any case' alcohol-impaired, regardless of actual driving behaviour?

options.a: 0.3 per mille
options.b: 0.5 per mille
options.c: 0.8 per mille
options.d: 1.6 per mille

at-alcohol-01.explanation: § 5(1) StVO fixes the irrebuttable presumption of impairment at 0.8 per mille blood alcohol (or 0.4 mg/l breath). The general driving limit already sits at 0.5 per mille (§ 14(8) FSG) — same number as Germany's § 24a StVG — but Austria's own presumption rule only kicks in at 0.8, whereas Germany's 'absolute Fahruntüchtigkeit' threshold is 1.1 per mille.

at-alcohol-02.question: Under § 4(7) FSG, what blood alcohol limit applies in Austria to holders of a probationary licence (Probeführerschein)?

options.a: 0.1 per mille
options.b: 0.0 per mille (a total alcohol ban)
options.c: 0.5 per mille, the same as everyone else
options.d: 0.3 per mille

at-alcohol-02.explanation: § 4(7) FSG allows probationary licence holders up to 0.1 per mille (0.05 mg/l breath). Germany is stricter here: under §§ 2a and 24c StVG, learner drivers in their probationary period and drivers under 21 face an absolute 0.0 per mille ban – the tempting but wrong answer to pick by analogy.

at-alcohol-03.question: Under § 4(1) FSG, how long is the probationary period (Probeführerschein) for a new car licence (class B) in Austria?

options.a: 2 years
options.b: 3 years
options.c: 1 year
options.d: 4 years

at-alcohol-03.explanation: § 4(1) FSG sets a three-year probationary period for all licence classes except AM and F. In Germany the probationary period under § 2a StVG lasts only two years – the tempting wrong answer by analogy.

at-alcohol-04.question: A probationary-licence holder commits a so-called 'Vormerkdelikt' (a registrable offence, e.g. drink-driving) during the Probezeit. What does § 4(3) FSG provide as the immediate consequence?

options.a: Immediate, permanent revocation of the licence
options.b: Only a fine; the probationary period continues unchanged
options.c: Points are added to a central national points account
options.d: The probationary period is extended by one further year and retraining (Nachschulung) is ordered

at-alcohol-04.explanation: § 4(3) FSG extends the probationary period by one year (or starts a fresh one-year period) after a Vormerkdelikt and orders a retraining course at the driver's expense. Germany instead runs a central points register (Fahreignungsregister) with a mandatory seminar triggered by point thresholds — a different mechanism from Austria's period-extension approach.

at-alcohol-05.question: A driver in Austria is stopped with a BAC of 1.7 per mille. How is this generally sanctioned under § 99(1) StVO?

options.a: Automatically as a court-prosecuted criminal offence
options.b: As an administrative offence with a fine of €1,600–€5,900 (or a substitute term of imprisonment)
options.c: Only with an on-the-spot fixed penalty ticket
options.d: With an automatic lifetime licence revocation and no further procedure

at-alcohol-05.explanation: Even the highest per-mille tier (from 1.6 ‰) is, under § 99(1)(a) StVO, an administrative offence carrying a fine of €1,600–€5,900 (or 2–6 weeks' substitute imprisonment if unpaid). In Germany, from 1.1 per mille ('absolute Fahruntüchtigkeit') the matter automatically becomes a criminal prosecution under § 316 StGB — a fundamentally different system.

at-alcohol-06.question: A driver in Austria refuses a roadside breath-alcohol test. Under § 99(1)(b) StVO, how is that refusal treated?

options.a: The same as the most severe alcohol offence, with the identical €1,600–€5,900 fine
options.b: More leniently than a positive result, since no measured value exists
options.c: Not punishable at all if the driver claims to be sober
options.d: Only with a warning on a first occasion

at-alcohol-06.explanation: § 99(1)(b) StVO equates refusing the breath test with the most severe per-mille tier, carrying the same €1,600–€5,900 fine. German law also sanctions refusal, but not automatically at the top fine of a specific per-mille band — it is handled as a separate offence with case-by-case evidentiary weight instead.

at-alcohol-07.question: In essence, what is Austria's 'Vormerksystem' under § 30a FSG?

options.a: A numeric points account that automatically revokes the licence at eight points
options.b: A purely civil-law register for traffic accidents
options.c: A register of specific, legally enumerated risk offences (e.g. alcohol, dangerous overtaking) which, if repeated within a two- or three-year window, triggers measures such as retraining or licence withdrawal, separately from any administrative fine
options.d: A system that applies only to professional drivers

at-alcohol-07.explanation: § 30a FSG lists specific 'Vormerkdelikte'; a second listed offence within two years (after which the observation window extends to three years) triggers separate measures such as retraining or withdrawal — in addition to whatever fine punishes the act itself. Germany has no direct equivalent: it runs a numeric points-based fitness register (the Flensburg points system) instead of a categorical offence list.

at-alcohol-08.question: What does § 14(1) FSG require an Austrian motor-vehicle driver to do on every journey?

options.a: Only carry the vehicle registration certificate; the driving licence itself may stay at home
options.b: Carry the required driving licence and hand it over for inspection on demand of the competent authorities
options.c: Carry an international driving permit in addition to the national one, even for domestic driving
options.d: There is no carrying duty at all, as long as identity can be proven with any ID card

at-alcohol-08.explanation: § 14(1) FSG requires carrying the driving licence and producing it to officials authorised to check it. This mirrors the basic German carrying duty (§ 4(2) no. 1 FeV in principle), but in Austria it sits directly in the FSG itself rather than in a separate driver-licensing ordinance.

at-alcohol-09.question: A driver in Austria has lost their driving licence and reported it immediately. Under § 14(3) FSG, for how long, at most, does the confirmation of that report entitle the driver to keep driving, counted from the day of the loss?

options.a: Two weeks
options.b: Until the vehicle's next roadworthiness inspection
options.c: Eight weeks
options.d: Indefinitely, until the replacement licence is delivered

at-alcohol-09.explanation: § 14(3) FSG expressly caps the entitlement to keep driving on a loss confirmation at eight weeks from the date of loss. Germany also issues a temporary replacement confirmation, but its validity period is not fixed nationwide at eight weeks by statute — it is set by the issuing authority.

at-alcohol-10.question: A driver in Austria is stopped with a BAC of 1.4 per mille. Which penalty tier of § 99 StVO applies, and what is the penalty range?

options.c: No penalty at all, since it is below 1.6 per mille
options.d: § 99(1a): €1,200–€4,400, or 10 days to 6 weeks' imprisonment if the fine cannot be recovered

at-alcohol-10.explanation: § 99(1a) StVO covers the 1.2-to-under-1.6-per-mille band with its own intermediate penalty tier (€1,200–€4,400, or 10 days to 6 weeks' substitute imprisonment) — unlike Germany, where below the 1.1 ‰ threshold of absolute unfitness a criminal offence under § 316 StGB usually requires additional signs of impaired driving, otherwise it remains a regulatory offence under § 24a StVG.

at-priority-01.question: At an intersection with no traffic lights, no priority signs, and no Vorrangstraße (priority road), two vehicles arrive at the same time. Under the StVO, who has priority?

options.a: The vehicle coming from the right
options.b: The vehicle coming from the left
options.c: The faster vehicle
options.d: The vehicle that reached the junction first

at-priority-01.explanation: § 19 Abs. 1 StVO establishes the basic right-of-way rule: traffic from the right has priority, unless a priority sign, a priority road, or a special case (such as rail vehicles) provides otherwise. This exactly matches the German 'right before left' rule (§ 8 StVO Germany) – there is no difference here.

at-priority-02.question: At an unsignposted intersection, a tram approaches from the left and a car approaches from the right. Under § 19 StVO, who has priority?

options.a: The car, because it comes from the right
options.b: The tram, because rail vehicles always have priority regardless of direction
options.c: Both must stop and negotiate with hand signals
options.d: The plain right-of-way rule applies; the tram has no special status

at-priority-02.explanation: § 19 Abs. 1 StVO makes an explicit exception to the right-of-way rule: rail vehicles have priority even when approaching from the left. This is identical to the German rule (§ 8 Abs. 1 StVO Germany) – again no divergence, but a common trap in exams.

at-priority-03.question: In Austria, a circular carriageway is marked with the regulatory sign for a Kreisverkehr (roundabout), but there is no additional priority sign at the entries. Does the roundabout sign itself establish that traffic already circulating has priority – the way the roundabout sign does in Germany?

options.a: Yes, as in Germany, the roundabout sign itself establishes priority for circulating traffic
options.b: No, under § 2 Abs. 1 Z 3c StVO the roundabout sign only describes the circular carriageway; priority is established by the separate priority signs (usually 'yield/give way') posted at each entry
options.c: No, in a roundabout circulating traffic must always give way to entering traffic
options.d: No, no priority rule applies at all in a roundabout, everyone proceeds at their own risk

at-priority-03.explanation: Unlike Germany, where the roundabout sign (Zeichen 215) itself establishes priority for the circulating carriageway, § 2 Abs. 1 Z 3c StVO defines a Kreisverkehr purely geometrically, as a circular carriageway for one-way traffic. In Austria, priority at a roundabout only comes from the separate priority signs posted at each entry under § 19 – in practice almost always 'yield', but legally this is a distinct arrangement. This is a genuine difference from Germany.

at-priority-04.question: A Vorrangstraße (priority road) crosses an ordinary road with no traffic lights. Under § 19 Abs. 3 StVO, who has priority?

options.a: Vehicles on the priority road, regardless of whether they come from the right or the left
options.b: The plain right-of-way rule still applies between the two roads
options.c: Vehicles on the priority road only if they additionally come from the right
options.d: Whichever driver enters the junction first

at-priority-04.explanation: § 19 Abs. 3 StVO gives vehicles on a priority road general priority over crossing or joining roads, regardless of direction. This matches the German concept of the Vorfahrtstraße (sign 306) – both countries agree here.

at-priority-05.question: A driver faces the regulatory sign 'yield / give way' before an intersection. Under § 19 Abs. 4 StVO, toward which vehicles at the intersection must she observe priority?

options.a: Only vehicles coming from the right, as the plain right-of-way rule would require
options.b: Toward every other vehicle at the intersection, regardless of whether it comes from the right or the left
options.c: Only rail vehicles
options.d: Toward no vehicle, the sign is only a non-binding hint

at-priority-05.explanation: § 19 Abs. 4 StVO provides that when 'yield' or 'stop' is posted before an intersection, both vehicles from the right and from the left have priority. So the plain right-of-way rule is fully suspended for the yielding approach – not just relative to traffic from the right. The practical result is the same in Germany.

at-priority-06.question: A vehicle exits a petrol station onto a road carrying through traffic; no priority sign is posted. Under § 19 Abs. 6 StVO, who has priority?

options.a: The exiting vehicle, if it is on the right
options.b: Through traffic on the road always has priority over a vehicle coming from the petrol station
options.c: Both must negotiate with hand signals who goes first
options.d: Plain right-before-left applies, as at any ordinary intersection

at-priority-06.explanation: § 19 Abs. 6 StVO explicitly lists parallel service roads, pedestrian zones, residential streets ('Wohnstraßen'), driveways, garages, car parks, petrol stations, and farm tracks: vehicles emerging from any of these must always give way to through traffic; the plain right-of-way rule does not apply here. Germany applies the same underlying idea via § 10 StVO ('whoever wants to enter the road must behave so that endangering others is excluded').

at-priority-07.question: A cyclist leaves a cycle path that is not continued as a marked cycle crossing, in order to move onto the roadway. Under § 19 Abs. 6a StVO, to whom must the cyclist give way?

options.a: No one; a cyclist leaving a cycle path always has priority
options.b: Vehicles in through traffic on the roadway
options.c: Only vehicles coming from the right
options.d: Only pedestrians on the footpath

at-priority-07.explanation: § 19 Abs. 6a StVO requires cyclists leaving a cycle path or combined foot/cycle path that is not continued by a marked cycle crossing to give way to through traffic. The underlying idea – no automatic priority for cyclists without a marked crossing – applies in much the same way in Germany.

at-priority-08.question: A driver without priority (the one required to yield) turns into a road. What does § 19 Abs. 7 StVO explicitly require?

options.a: He may turn in as long as he sounds the horn or signals
options.b: He must not force the drivers of vehicles with priority into sudden braking or swerving
options.c: He must come to a complete stop even if no other traffic is in sight
options.d: He may turn in if his vehicle can accelerate faster than the one with priority

at-priority-08.explanation: § 19 Abs. 7 StVO requires the yielding driver not to force those with priority into sudden braking or swerving. This duty corresponds in substance to § 11 Abs. 3 StVO Germany – again no divergence, just a different paragraph number.

at-priority-09.question: A driver with priority waves a yielding vehicle to go first. Is such a waiver of priority permitted under § 19 Abs. 8 StVO?

options.a: No, waiving priority is generally not permitted in Austria
options.b: Yes, she may waive her priority, but she must make this clearly recognizable to the yielding driver
options.c: Yes, but a waiver of priority is only permitted toward rail vehicles
options.d: Yes, any gesture counts as a valid waiver, even if the yielding driver never perceives it

at-priority-09.explanation: § 19 Abs. 8 StVO explicitly allows a driver with priority to waive it, but requires that the waiver be made clearly recognizable to the yielding driver – a mere sign that is never perceived is not enough. This clarification is explicitly codified in the StVO; in Germany the same practical rule applies, just without being spelled out as explicitly in the statute text.

at-priority-10.question: An emergency vehicle with blue lights approaches an intersection at the same time as an ordinary car coming from the left. Under § 19 Abs. 2 StVO, who has priority?

options.a: The emergency vehicle always has priority
options.b: The plain right-of-way rule still applies between the two vehicles
options.c: The emergency vehicle only has priority if it comes from the right
options.d: The emergency vehicle only has priority outside built-up areas

at-priority-10.explanation: § 19 Abs. 2 StVO states directly within the priority rules: emergency vehicles (§ 2 Abs. 1 Z 25) always have priority, regardless of direction or built-up area. This is phrased as its own paragraph inside the priority rules – in Germany, the priority of emergency vehicles instead follows from the general duty to immediately clear a path for them (§ 38 StVO Germany), without a dedicated priority clause inside the right-before-left provision.

at-signs-01.question: In an Austrian Begegnungszone (encounter/shared-space zone), what is the default maximum speed for vehicles unless the authority orders otherwise?

options.a: 20 km/h
options.b: 30 km/h
options.c: Walking pace, the same as in a Wohnstraße
options.d: 50 km/h, the normal urban limit

at-signs-01.explanation: § 76c(1) StVO fixes the default Begegnungszone speed at 20 km/h, which the authority may raise to 30 km/h by ordinance. German traffic law has no equivalent zone; its closest relative, the verkehrsberuhigter Bereich (traffic-calmed area, sign 325), requires walking pace (roughly 7 km/h), not 20 km/h.

at-signs-02.question: What is the speed limit for permitted vehicle traffic inside an Austrian Wohnstraße (residential street)?

options.a: Walking pace
options.b: 20 km/h
options.c: 30 km/h
options.d: A fixed 10 km/h

at-signs-02.explanation: § 76b(5) StVO requires walking pace throughout a Wohnstraße. This is not an Austrian quirk: Germany's verkehrsberuhigter Bereich (sign 325) imposes exactly the same walking-pace rule.

at-signs-03.question: Under § 76b StVO, who may drive a motor vehicle into a street marked as a Wohnstraße?

options.a: Only traffic accessing or leaving a destination within it, plus cyclists and certain service/emergency vehicles
options.b: Anyone, as long as they keep to walking pace
options.c: Only residents holding a special permit from the authority
options.d: No one at all — the sign acts as an absolute ban with no exceptions

at-signs-03.explanation: An Austrian Wohnstraße is not simply a speed-limited zone open to everyone — general through motor traffic is excluded outright; only access/egress traffic, cyclists, and listed service vehicles may enter. A German driver would naturally assume otherwise, because Germany's verkehrsberuhigter Bereich (sign 325) really does admit all traffic, just at walking pace.

at-signs-04.question: Where does Austrian law fix the design and legal meaning of traffic signs?

options.a: Directly within the StVO 1960 itself, in §§ 50 to 55
options.b: In a separate traffic-signs ordinance, apart from the StVO
options.c: In annexes to the StVO, the way Germany does it
options.d: Only in ÖNORM technical standards, with no statutory basis

at-signs-04.explanation: Austria codifies danger signs (§ 50), regulatory signs (§ 52), information signs (§ 53), supplementary plates (§ 54) and road markings (§ 55) directly in the StVO's own running text. Germany does the opposite: its StVO only names the sign categories, while each sign's actual design and legal effect sit in Anlage 1 to 4 of the StVO.

at-signs-05.question: The Schulstraße ("school street") information sign (§ 53 no. 26a StVO) marks a street with restricted access around a school. How does this relate to German law?

options.a: The German StVO has no dedicated sign for it; German school streets are set up, if at all, with movable barriers or one-off traffic orders
options.b: It corresponds exactly to German sign 250, "no vehicles of any kind"
options.c: It is identical to the German pedestrian-zone sign (242.1)
options.d: It corresponds to Germany's 30 km/h zone sign posted near schools

at-signs-05.explanation: Austria has a dedicated, named information sign (no. 26a) for school streets with a fixed statutory meaning. Germany's StVO annexes have no matching sign category; German cities that run "Schulstraßen" do so through ad hoc traffic orders using existing signs and barriers, not a purpose-built sign.

at-signs-06.question: Under Austrian law, how long may the combined red-and-yellow phase of a traffic light last at most?

options.a: At most 2 seconds
options.b: At most 5 seconds
options.c: The law sets no maximum duration
options.d: Exactly 3 seconds, fixed by statute

at-signs-06.explanation: § 38(2) StVO expressly caps the combined red-and-yellow phase at 2 seconds — a number the German statute itself does not spell out. The signal's meaning is the same in both countries: "stop", with green about to follow.

at-signs-07.question: Under § 38 StVO, what often happens at an Austrian traffic light just before green switches to yellow?

options.a: The green light flashes four times, 0.5 seconds each, warning that the green phase is about to end
options.b: Nothing in particular — as in Germany, green switches straight to yellow with no warning
options.c: The yellow light already flashes alongside the green during the green phase
options.d: An audible tone replaces any visual warning

at-signs-07.explanation: Austria may end a green phase with four 0.5-second flashes of the green light as an advance warning. German traffic lights have no such feature: green switches straight to solid yellow without any flashing warning.

at-signs-08.question: Under what condition may cyclists in Austria turn right or go straight on a red light?

options.a: Only where a bicycle-specific supplementary device permits it, and only after coming to a full stop first
options.b: Always, as long as no oncoming traffic is near, even without any extra sign
options.c: Only under the general green-arrow sign, which applies to all vehicles as it does in Germany
options.d: Never — cyclists must stay fully stopped at red like every other road user

at-signs-08.explanation: § 38 StVO permits this red-light exception for cyclists only where a bicycle-specific supplementary device authorizes it, and only after a full stop. That is narrower than Germany's Grünpfeil (sign 720), which applies to all vehicle types, not just bicycles.

at-signs-09.question: What color does § 55 StVO prescribe for the road marking of a Kurzparkzone (short-term/paid-disc parking zone)?

options.a: Blue
options.b: White, like most other markings
options.c: Yellow, as used for construction sites
options.d: Red-and-white stripes

at-signs-09.explanation: § 55(6) StVO reserves blue paint specifically for Kurzparkzone markings; markings are otherwise white, and temporary construction-related markings are yellow. Germany has no comparable blue road marking for its disc-parking (Parkscheibenpflicht) zones — there, signage alone does the job.

at-signs-10.question: What effect does the Austrian regulatory sign "Vorrangstraße" (priority road, § 52 no. 25a StVO) have?

options.a: It gives the marked road priority over joining traffic until the "end of priority road" sign — the same as Germany's Vorfahrtstraße (sign 306)
options.b: It suspends the right-of-way rule for the whole town
options.c: It applies only to motor vehicles, not to cyclists
options.d: It replaces traffic lights at every subsequent intersection

at-signs-10.explanation: There is no real difference from Germany here: Austria's Vorrangstraße works exactly like the German Vorfahrtstraße — continuous priority over joining roads until the end-of-sign marker, regardless of vehicle type.

at-speed-01.question: What is the general speed limit on an Autobahn (motorway) in Austria where no lower limit is posted?

options.a: There is no general limit, only an advisory speed of 130 km/h
options.b: 130 km/h as a binding statutory limit
options.c: 120 km/h as a binding statutory limit
options.d: 100 km/h, the same as on an ordinary rural road

at-speed-01.explanation: § 20(2) StVO fixes 130 km/h as a binding statutory limit on Austrian motorways. That is the key contrast with Germany, where there is no general statutory Autobahn limit at all, only a non-binding advisory speed of 130 km/h.

at-speed-02.question: A German driver is on an Austrian Schnellstraße (S-road, expressway) outside a built-up area that looks almost like a motorway. What speed limit applies there without extra signage?

options.a: 130 km/h, because a Schnellstraße counts as an Autobahn
options.b: 80 km/h, because Schnellstraßen are regulated more strictly than ordinary rural roads
options.c: 100 km/h, the same as any other rural road
options.d: No limit at all, since Schnellstraßen are treated like unrestricted Kraftfahrstraßen

at-speed-02.explanation: Only Autobahnen get the 130 km/h figure under § 20(2) StVO; every other rural road, including a Schnellstraße unless signed otherwise, stays at the 100 km/h general rural limit. The visual resemblance to a motorway is exactly the trap for a visiting driver.

at-speed-03.question: Under what reason, named explicitly in the StVO, may an Austrian municipality set a limit below 50 km/h for its whole built-up area (Ortsgebiet) by ordinance?

options.a: Because of persistently elevated noise or pollutant exposure across the whole area
options.b: Only if a federal highway runs through the built-up area
options.c: Only on school days between 7 and 8 a.m.
options.d: Only after a local referendum has been held

at-speed-03.explanation: § 20(2a) StVO explicitly lists persistently elevated noise or pollutant exposure as grounds for an area-wide reduction below 50 km/h. Germany also allows area-wide Tempo 30 for noise or air-quality reasons, but it rests on the general ordering power of the traffic authority rather than a dedicated statutory clause like this one.

at-speed-04.question: A moped with a design speed of 45 km/h wants to use an Austrian Autobahn. Is that allowed?

options.a: Yes, as long as it never actually exceeds 130 km/h
options.b: No, the StVO requires a design speed of at least 60 km/h to use a motorway
options.c: Yes, but only on the hard shoulder
options.d: No, only passenger cars are permitted on motorways at all

at-speed-04.explanation: § 46(1) StVO restricts motorway use to motor vehicles with a design speed of at least 60 km/h, so the moped is excluded regardless of how it is actually driven. Germany applies the identical 60 km/h threshold under § 18 StVO — one of the rare cases where the two rules line up exactly.

at-speed-05.question: On a motorway section with three or more lanes per direction, may a truck with a maximum permissible mass over 7,500 kg use the outermost left lane?

options.a: No, in general, except to change direction at an intersection or junction
options.b: Yes, without restriction, like any other vehicle
options.c: Only at night between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.
options.d: Only if it is capable of exceeding 100 km/h

at-speed-05.explanation: § 46(4a) StVO generally bars trucks over 7,500 kg from the outermost left lane on three-or-more-lane motorway sections. Germany has no comparable blanket statutory rule; there, the left lane is closed to heavy trucks only where a local sign (Zeichen 277) says so, not by a nationwide StVO rule with a fixed weight and lane-count threshold.

at-speed-06.question: Where does the Austrian StVO expressly set the duty to form a Rettungsgasse (emergency corridor) when traffic stalls?

options.a: In a dedicated section on behaviour toward emergency vehicles inside built-up areas
options.b: Nowhere; in Austria it is only a motoring-club recommendation with no legal force
options.c: In the Autobahnen paragraph, § 46, for a carriageway with at least two lanes in one direction
options.d: Only in a separate ministerial ordinance, not in the StVO itself

at-speed-06.explanation: In Austria the Rettungsgasse duty sits in § 46(6) StVO, inside the Autobahnen section. In Germany the equivalent duty (§ 11(2) StVO) instead sits among the general traffic-behaviour rules and applies expressly on any multi-lane road outside built-up areas, not only on the motorway.

at-speed-07.question: Under § 46(6) StVO, who may use the emergency corridor kept clear on the motorway?

options.a: Only police, fire brigade, and ambulance vehicles
options.b: Emergency vehicles plus road-maintenance and breakdown-assistance vehicles, and no one else
options.c: Any vehicle wanting to bypass the jam, as long as it drives carefully
options.d: Emergency vehicles, road-service vehicles, breakdown-assistance vehicles, and hearses

at-speed-07.explanation: Austria's StVO, in § 46(6), expressly names hearses as entitled to use the emergency corridor too — an unusually specific list. Germany's equivalent, § 11(2) StVO, names police, fire brigade, rescue services and the road authority's own vehicles, but does not list hearses.

at-speed-08.question: On some Austrian motorway sections you see signs marked "IG-L" under a reduced speed figure. What law is that restriction based on?

options.a: The StVO, § 20, the same as any other speed limit
options.b: The Immissionsschutzgesetz-Luft (IG-L), a dedicated air-pollution-control act
options.c: The Kraftfahrgesetz, because it concerns vehicles' design speed
options.d: A voluntary commitment by the motorway operator ASFINAG

at-speed-08.explanation: These so-called "Lufthunderter" limits rest on § 14 IG-L, not the StVO — authorities order them to avoid breaching air-quality thresholds. German law has no equivalent standalone air-quality act with its own speed-limiting power; it addresses air pollution through low-emission zones and driving bans instead of dedicated speed limits.

at-speed-09.question: Who is expressly exempted from a speed restriction ordered under the IG-L?

options.a: Zero-emission vehicles (e.g. fully electric vehicles), under the conditions the act sets out
options.b: All vehicles carrying an Austrian number plate
options.c: All vehicles travelling before 9 p.m.
options.d: No one; IG-L limits apply to every vehicle without exception

at-speed-09.explanation: § 14 IG-L names zero-emission vehicles as a group exempted from such restrictions, since they do not cause the air pollutants the measure targets. German law has no comparable vehicle-specific exemption from an air-quality speed limit, because it has no equivalent to the IG-L at all.

at-speed-10.question: For how long may an IG-L speed restriction on a motorway or expressway be ordered without needing the competent federal minister's separate agreement (mere notification is enough)?

options.a: Indefinitely; agreement is never required
options.b: At most one week
options.c: At most three months
options.d: At most one year

at-speed-10.explanation: Under § 14 IG-L, for motorways and expressways a restriction lasting up to three months only needs notification to the transport ministry; anything longer needs its actual agreement. German law has no comparable tiered, environmentally-grounded approval procedure for speed limits, since it has no IG-L counterpart.

at-vulnerable_users-01.question: An inline skater wants to cross the road at an unsignalised Schutzweg (zebra crossing) in Austria. Under § 9 StVO 1960, must a driver let them cross unobstructed?

options.a: Yes — § 9 StVO 1960 explicitly names both pedestrians AND roller skaters, so the same priority covers both.
options.b: No — the rule only protects pedestrians; skaters get no special priority at a Schutzweg.
options.c: No — inline skaters are not legally allowed to use a Schutzweg at all.
options.d: Yes, but only if the Schutzweg is additionally controlled by traffic lights.

at-vulnerable_users-01.explanation: § 9(2) StVO 1960 explicitly obliges drivers toward 'a pedestrian or roller skater'. Germany's equivalent, § 26 StVO, only mentions pedestrians at the Fußgängerüberweg and does not explicitly extend the same right to skaters. So in Austria, unlike Germany, skaters are named right in the statute.

at-vulnerable_users-02.question: A cyclist, without dismounting, wants to cross a marked Radfahrerüberfahrt (bicycle crossing) next to a junction. What is the priority situation towards a driver under § 9 StVO 1960?

options.a: The cyclist, just like a pedestrian at a Schutzweg, is entitled to cross unobstructed and unendangered — they do not need to dismount.
options.b: The cyclist must dismount and push the bicycle across, otherwise the driver has priority.
options.c: A Radfahrerüberfahrt is governed by the general right-before-left rule, regardless of cycle or car traffic.
options.d: The cyclist only has priority if a pedestrian is crossing the adjoining Schutzweg at the same time.

at-vulnerable_users-02.explanation: § 9 StVO 1960 explicitly extends the Schutzweg priority to cyclists at a Radfahrerüberfahrt while they remain seated. In Germany, a cyclist at a comparable crossing furrow does not automatically enjoy the same protected status — many German drivers assume (incorrectly from an Austrian standpoint) that a cyclist must dismount to be treated like a pedestrian.

at-vulnerable_users-03.question: In an Austrian built-up area (Ortsgebiet), a Schutzweg is located 20 metres from a pedestrian. May she still cross the road right where she is standing?

options.a: No — where a Schutzweg or pedestrian subway is within 25 metres in a built-up area, it must be used.
options.b: Yes — pedestrians may cross anywhere in a built-up area as long as it is safe to do so.
options.c: No — outside a Schutzweg, crossing is never permitted anywhere in Austria.
options.d: Yes, but only if she crosses at a 45-degree angle.

at-vulnerable_users-03.explanation: § 76(4) StVO 1960 obliges pedestrians in a built-up area to use a Schutzweg (or pedestrian under/overpass) if it is within 25 metres. German law has no such fixed metre threshold; it only requires using a crossing that is 'reasonably close', without a defined distance.

at-vulnerable_users-04.question: A 13-year-old child, 145 cm tall, is travelling in a car. What does § 106(5) KFG 1967 require?

options.a: The child still needs a suitable child restraint system matched to size and weight, because they are under 150 cm and under 14 years old.
options.b: An ordinary seatbelt is enough, because the child is already older than 12.
options.c: The child must be carried rear-facing until their 14th birthday.
options.d: A restraint system is only required up to a height of 135 cm.

at-vulnerable_users-04.explanation: Austria ties the child-restraint duty to a height of 150 cm and an age ceiling of 14 (§ 106(5) KFG 1967). Germany's equivalent, § 21(1a) StVO, sets the age ceiling at just 12 (also combined with under 150 cm). A 13-year-old but small child would no longer need a child seat in Germany, but still would in Austria.

at-vulnerable_users-05.question: In Austria, a physically separated, signed Radweg (cycle path) runs alongside a road. A cyclist approaches, towing a 90 cm-wide trailer. What does § 68 StVO 1960 require?

options.a: They must use the cycle path, because their trailer is no wider than 100 cm.
options.b: They may not use the cycle path at all, because towing any trailer always excludes the duty to use it.
options.c: Austria has no general duty to use a marked cycle path — cycling on the roadway is always optional.
options.d: They may choose freely, since the duty to use the cycle path only applies to racing bikes.

at-vulnerable_users-05.explanation: § 68(1) StVO 1960 makes a signed cycle path mandatory for single-track bicycles; trailers up to 100 cm wide don't change that — only wider trailers or overly wide multi-track cycles must move to the roadway. Germany has a similar mandatory-cycle-path duty (blue sign), but its exception is not tied to this specific 100 cm trailer-width threshold.

at-vulnerable_users-06.question: A 10-year-old girl is cycling on the road in Austria on an ordinary bicycle, without a helmet. Is that allowed?

options.a: No — under § 68(6) StVO 1960, children under 12 must wear a crash helmet.
options.b: Yes — Austria, like Germany, has no legal helmet requirement for cyclists.
options.c: Yes, because in Austria the helmet duty only starts at age 14.
options.d: No, but only because she isn't riding an e-bike.

at-vulnerable_users-06.explanation: § 68(6) StVO 1960 requires children under 12 to wear a crash helmet on any bicycle (for certain e-bikes the duty even extends to under 14). Germany, by contrast, has no legal helmet requirement for cyclists at all, not even for children — there it remains a recommendation only.

at-vulnerable_users-07.question: A driver wants to drive through a street marked 'Wohnstraße' (residential street) in Austria to reach their garage. What rules apply there under § 76b StVO 1960?

options.a: They may enter and exit for access purposes, but must drive at walking pace and must not obstruct or endanger playing children or cyclists.
options.b: Driving a motor vehicle through a Wohnstraße is generally forbidden for everyone, even just to enter or exit.
options.c: They may drive at normal speed as long as no children are currently visible.
options.d: A Wohnstraße is a pure pedestrian zone where no vehicle traffic whatsoever is allowed.

at-vulnerable_users-07.explanation: In a Wohnstraße, vehicle traffic is generally prohibited, with exceptions including cycling and access traffic to properties — but that access traffic must proceed at walking pace, and pedestrians are even allowed to use the roadway and play there. Germany has a broadly similar concept with the 'verkehrsberuhigter Bereich' (traffic-calmed zone, sign 325), but under a different name and with somewhat different through-traffic exceptions.

at-vulnerable_users-08.question: A section of road in Austria has been designated a 'Begegnungszone' (encounter zone) without any extra posted speed. What maximum speed applies to vehicles there under § 76c StVO 1960?

options.a: 20 km/h, unless the authority has expressly permitted up to 30 km/h.
options.b: 30 km/h, as in a German traffic-calmed zone.
options.c: 10 km/h, the same as in a Wohnstraße.
options.d: No speed limit applies at all, since pedestrians have priority anyway.

at-vulnerable_users-08.explanation: § 76c StVO 1960 sets the default speed in an Austrian Begegnungszone at 20 km/h; the authority may authorise up to 30 km/h by ordinance. The Begegnungszone is a distinctly Austrian concept — pedestrians may use the full width of the street and have priority, but must not deliberately obstruct vehicle traffic. Germany has no direct equivalent in this form.

at-vulnerable_users-09.question: A driver with a valid pass under § 29b StVO 1960 (disability parking pass) wants to park in a short-term parking zone without observing the zone's normal maximum parking duration. Is that allowed?

options.a: Yes — holders of a § 29b pass may park in short-term parking zones without the time limit that otherwise applies.
options.b: No — even with the pass, the normal maximum parking duration applies just like to everyone else.
options.c: No — the pass is valid only on dedicated disabled-parking bays marked with their own symbol.
options.d: Yes, but only on Sundays and public holidays.

at-vulnerable_users-09.explanation: § 29b StVO 1960 entitles pass holders to park in short-term parking zones without the usual maximum duration, and also in areas with stopping/parking bans (subject to displaying the pass visibly). Germany's blue EU disabled parking permit grants broadly similar but detail-different relief, for instance around time-limited parking in disabled bays.

at-vulnerable_users-10.question: Since 1 May 2026, a new rule has applied to e-scooters in Austria. How are e-scooters now legally classified?

options.a: As their own vehicle category ('Rollerfahren', § 68a StVO 1960) with its own set of rules, no longer simply treated as an ordinary bicycle.
options.b: They continue to count fully as bicycles and remain subject to exactly the same rules as § 68 StVO 1960.
options.c: They now count as motor vehicles requiring a driving licence and number plate, like a moped.
options.d: E-scooters have been generally banned from public roads in Austria since then.

at-vulnerable_users-10.explanation: Under the StVO amendment BGBl. I Nr. 17/2026, e-scooters (§ 2(1) no. 22a StVO 1960) got their own new § 68a ('Rollerfahren') instead of continuing to be treated simply as bicycles — including their own helmet duty up to age 16 and a 0.5 per mille alcohol limit. Germany has for some time also classified e-scooters (Elektrokleinstfahrzeuge) as their own vehicle category under the eKFV, likewise not as bicycles — so a German driver expecting 'treated like a bicycle' has been wrong for Austria too, since May 2026.
